_sources.taxable_scholarship: U.S.-China treaty, Article 20(b): a student resident of China is exempt on 'grants or awards from a government, scientific, educational or other tax-exempt organization' (treaty text, irs.gov/pub/irs-trty/china.pdf). A university scholarship paid by the educational institution itself falls squarely inside 20(b) and carries NO dollar cap (the $5,000 cap in 20(c) applies only to personal-services income). The 1042-S marks the exemption (exemption code 04, Instructions for Form 1042-S). Modeling note: amounts NOT exempt under a treaty would go to Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8r, per the Instructions for Form 1040-NR (2025), Line 1a TIP.

description: NR-004: Chinese F-1 student with W-2 wages $6,500 (all on the W-2, so the Article 20(c) $5,000 exemption is claimed on the return) PLUS a $4,000 university scholarship on Form 1042-S (income code 15, exemption code 04). The scholarship is a grant from an educational organization, so U.S.-China treaty Article 20(b) exempts it in full (no dollar cap) — it is NOT routed to taxable scholarship: taxable_scholarship = 0, and line 1k carries BOTH treaty-exempt amounts ($5,000 under 20(c) + $4,000 under 20(b) = $9,000, two Schedule OI entries). Taxable wages $1,500; refund $49.
